kin.title: Velocity is a slope, and velocities add as arrows
kin.mini: The mean velocity is the distance covered divided by the time taken: the slope of the chord on a graph of position against time. Velocities are vectors: an airliner's ground speed is its airspeed plus the wind, end to end.
kin.text: Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it. Δ (delta) means “the change in”: Δx is the distance covered between two instants, Δt the time between them, and their ratio is the mean velocity over that interval, the slope of the straight chord joining two points of the graph of x against t. Acceleration is the same thing one level up: the change in velocity over the time. Position, velocity and acceleration are vectors: they have a size and a direction, and adding two of them means putting the arrows end to end. 900 km/h going east and 900 km/h going west are two different velocities; an airliner's ground speed is its airspeed plus the wind, added as arrows, and the length of an arrow follows from Pythagoras.
kin.labels: Mean velocity: the slope of the chord|Vectors add end to end
galileo.title: Why a smooth motion cannot be felt
galileo.mini: Seen from a train at constant speed V, positions and speeds change by V t and V, but accelerations do not. Forces give accelerations, so physics is the same in both frames: what is felt is acceleration, never speed.
galileo.text: A frame of reference is an observer with axes and a clock. It is inertial when a body on which no force acts moves in a straight line at constant speed. Galileo noticed in 1632 that in the closed cabin of a ship sailing smoothly, flies, fish in a bowl and falling drops behave exactly as on land: no experiment inside tells uniform motion from rest [1]. Measured from a train moving at constant speed V, a position is x′ = x − V t and a velocity v′ = v − V, but the acceleration is the same, because V is constant and vanishes when differentiated. Forces, which give accelerations, are therefore the same in every inertial frame. That is why “I would feel the Earth move” is not an argument: a body feels accelerations, not speeds.
rotframe.title: In a turning frame, straight lines curve: Coriolis
rotframe.mini: Roll a ball straight across a turning disc: seen from outside it goes straight, seen from the disc it curves. To keep Newton's laws, the turning frame adds two inertial forces, Coriolis and centrifugal. The Earth's are small but measured.
rotframe.text: A rotating frame is not inertial. On a merry-go-round, a ball rolled straight across seems to curve and a passenger feels pushed outwards, although nothing pushes. Written in the turning frame, Newton's second law only works if two inertial forces are added, which come from the frame's own rotation and not from another body [1]: the Coriolis acceleration 2 Ω v sin φ, across the motion, to the right in the northern hemisphere, and the centrifugal acceleration Ω² r, away from the axis. The ground turns once a sidereal day, Ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s [2], so these forces are small: the Coriolis acceleration on an airliner at 250 m/s at 45° is {{cor}} m/s², {{corPct}} % of gravity, and the centrifugal acceleration at the equator {{aEq}} m/s². Foucault pendulums, ring lasers, gyroscopes and gravimeters measure them. In the drawing the disc's rotation is exaggerated.
newton.title: Newton's laws: force sets acceleration, and every push is mutual
newton.mini: The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration; with no net force it keeps its speed. When the Earth pulls an apple down, the apple pulls the Earth up just as hard.
newton.text: Newton's three laws (1687) [1]. First: a body stays at rest or in uniform straight motion unless a force acts on it. Second: the sum of the forces equals the mass times the acceleration, ΣF = m a; the first law is the second with no net force, as for a book at rest on a desk, whose weight and the desk's push cancel. Third: when a body pushes another, the other pushes back with an equal and opposite force. The apple pulls the Earth up exactly as hard as the Earth pulls the apple down; the Earth's acceleration is invisible because its mass is 10²⁴ times larger, and the two forces never cancel because they act on different bodies. Mass, in kilograms, measures how hard a body is to accelerate and is the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on it, m g, in newtons, and changes with g.
newton.labels: Second law: a = ΣF / m|Third law: equal and opposite
grav.title: The same gravity drops the apple and holds the Moon
grav.mini: Gravity falls as the square of the distance. The Moon, 60 Earth radii away, must fall {{moonOrbit}} mm/s² to stay on its orbit; surface gravity weakened 3,600 times gives {{moonG}}. Newton's test, 1687.
grav.text: Every pair of masses attracts along the line joining them, with a force G m₁ m₂ / r² that falls as the square of the distance between their centres. G was first measured in the laboratory by Cavendish in 1798, with lead spheres on a torsion balance [2]. At the surface of a sphere of mass M and radius R the acceleration is g = GM/R²: {{gSph}} m/s² for the Earth's GM [3] and a radius of 6,371 km. Newton's test [1]: the Moon, at 60 Earth radii, goes round in 27.32 days [4]; to bend its path into that circle it must fall towards the Earth by {{moonOrbit}} mm/s². Gravity at the surface, weakened by (1/60)² = 1/3,600, gives {{moonG}} mm/s². They agree to {{moonPct}} %, and to better with the Moon's own mass counted (G(M+m): {{moonGpair}} mm/s²). One force makes apples fall and keeps the Moon in orbit. The Moon's fall is enlarged in the drawing.
grav.labels: Gravitation: F = G m₁ m₂ / r²|The Moon falls towards the Earth
circ.title: Turning at constant speed is accelerating
circ.mini: Every point of a turning body has the same angular velocity ω, but goes faster the farther it is from the axis: v = ω r. Its velocity keeps changing direction, so it accelerates towards the centre: a = ω² r, {{aEq}} m/s² at the equator.
circ.text: Angular velocity ω is how fast an angle turns, in radians per second: ω = 2π/T for one turn in a time T. Every point of a turning body has the same ω, but its speed v = ω r grows with its distance r from the axis. For the Earth ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s [1], one turn relative to the stars in {{tSid}} s. Turning at constant speed is accelerating: the speed keeps its size but not its direction, and between two instants the difference Δv of the velocity arrows points to the centre. That centripetal acceleration, v²/r = ω² r, has to be provided by a force, the string of a sling or gravity for the Moon [2]; seen from the turning frame it appears as the centrifugal force. At the equator ω² R = {{aEq}} m/s², {{aEqPct}} % of g.
circ.labels: Angular velocity: v = ω r|Centripetal acceleration: ω² r
sidereal.title: Two kinds of day: why the stars rise four minutes earlier
sidereal.mini: The solar day, noon to noon, is 86,400 s. Relative to the stars the Earth turns in {{tSidCalc}} s: because it also moves along its orbit, it must turn a bit more each day to face the Sun again. 366.24 turns for 365.24 noons.
sidereal.text: The solar day, 86,400 s from noon to noon, is a turn of the Earth relative to the Sun; the sidereal day is a turn relative to the stars. Because the Earth also moves along its orbit, it has to turn a little more than once to face the Sun again: in a year it turns 366.24 times relative to the stars for 365.24 noons. Hence 1/T_sid = 1/T_sol + 1/T_year, which gives T_sid = {{tSidCalc}} s, the value the IERS uses for the Earth's rotation [1]. That is why a star sets behind the same chimney 3 min 56 s earlier every night, and why the constellations of the evening sky change with the seasons. In the drawing, the Earth's motion along its orbit in one day is enlarged.
conserv.title: What does not change: energy and momentum
conserv.mini: A falling ball trades height for speed, ½mv² + mgh staying constant: it lands at √(2gh) whatever its mass. Two skaters pushing apart keep a total momentum of zero, so the lighter one leaves faster.
conserv.text: In an isolated system some totals stay constant whatever happens inside; they follow from Newton's laws [1] and often give the answer directly. Energy: a ball dropped from a height h trades potential energy mgh for kinetic energy ½mv², their sum staying the same, so it reaches the ground at v = √(2gh) whatever its mass. Far from the ground, where g is no longer constant, the potential energy is −GMm/r. Momentum, mass times velocity: two skaters at rest push each other apart; the total momentum was zero and stays zero, so a skater half as heavy leaves twice as fast, the opposite way. A rocket works the same way with its exhaust gases, which is why it needs no air to push against.
kepler.title: Kepler's laws: equal areas, and T² as a³
kepler.mini: A planet sweeps equal areas in equal times, fast near the Sun, slow far from it. The square of the period grows as the cube of the orbit's size: a GPS satellite at 26,560 km goes round in {{tGps}} h, the Moon in {{tMoonPair}} days.
kepler.text: Kepler's second law (1609): the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps equal areas in equal times [1]. Newton showed it is the conservation of angular momentum, L = m r² θ̇, under a force aimed at the Sun [2]: close in, the planet turns faster. The Earth is fastest in early January, at perihelion. Kepler's third law (1619), as Newton derived it from the inverse square: T² = 4π² a³ / G(M+m), the square of the period grows as the cube of the orbit's semi-major axis. Four times farther takes eight times longer. With the Earth's GM [3], a GPS satellite at a = 26,560 km goes round in {{tGps}} h, half a sidereal day; the Moon, at 384,400 km [4], in {{tMoon}} days with GM alone and {{tMoonPair}} days with its own mass counted, against {{tMoonObs}} observed. The ellipse's eccentricity is exaggerated in the drawing.
kepler.labels: Second law: equal areas in equal times|Third law: T² ∝ a³
waves.title: Waves: wavelength, frequency, and the Doppler shift
waves.mini: In one period a wave advances one wavelength: v = λ f. A source moving away stretches its waves and its frequency drops; one coming closer raises it. Only the speed along the line of sight counts: Δf/f ≈ −v_r/c.
waves.text: A wave carries energy without carrying matter: the sea swell, sound, seismic waves, radio and light are all disturbances that travel while each point only oscillates about its place. The wavelength λ is the distance between two crests, the frequency f the number of crests passing per second; in one period T = 1/f the wave advances one wavelength, so v = λ f, and the travel time over a distance d is d/v. The Doppler effect (1842) [1]: a source moving away stretches its waves, so the frequency received drops; one coming closer squeezes them, so it rises. That is the change in pitch of a passing siren. For speeds small compared with the wave's, Δf/f ≈ −v_r/c, where v_r is the speed along the line of sight only. Measured on starlight it gives the Earth's orbital speed; on satellite radio signals, their orbits. The source's speed is exaggerated in the drawing.
waves.labels: v = λ f|Doppler: fronts squeezed ahead
snell.title: Refraction: light bends where it slows down
snell.mini: Passing into a medium where it is slower, light bends towards the perpendicular: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Air thins with height, so a nearly level ray bends gently downward: atmospheric refraction.
snell.text: Light goes at c in vacuum and slower in matter; the refractive index n = c/v says how much slower: 1.000 for air at the surface (1.0003 more precisely), 1.333 for water. When a ray passes into a medium where it is slower, it bends towards the perpendicular to the surface, following the law of sines n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, written by Descartes in 1637 and found earlier by Snellius and Ibn Sahl [1]. The drawing has the true angles for 50° in air: 35° in water. Air gets thinner with height, so its index slowly decreases upwards and a ray going nearly level bends gently downward, following the curve of the Earth a little: that is atmospheric refraction. It lifts what is seen near the horizon by a fraction of a degree and varies with the temperature of the air.
const.title: Constants: some define the units, g is not one of them
const.mini: Since 2019 the metre is the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 s, so c is exact by definition. G is measured. g is local: from {{gPole}} m/s² at the poles to {{gEq}} at the equator. 9.80665 is only a convention.
const.text: Not every “constant” is the same kind of number. The seven constants of the SI are exact by definition: since 2019 the second is 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the caesium-133 atom and the metre the distance light travels in 1/299,792,458 of that second, so the speed of light can no longer be measured, only used [1]. The gravitational constant G is universal and measured, the least well known of all, to 2 parts in 100,000 [2]. The Earth's GM, its rotation and its radius are properties of one planet. g is local: on a turning sphere the centrifugal term lowers it from {{gPoleSph}} m/s² at the poles to {{gEqSph}} at the equator; measured, it goes from {{gPole}} to {{gEq}} m/s² [3], the rest coming from the Earth's flattening. The “standard” g = 9.80665 m/s² was adopted in 1901 for weighing [4]: a convention, not a value found anywhere in particular. In the drawing the centrifugal arrow is enlarged.
const.labels: A constant defines the metre|g changes with latitude
forcetable.title: Adding forces: the force table
forcetable.mini: Three ropes over pulleys pull a ring with 3, 4 and 5 kg. The ring slides along the sum of the forces until that sum is zero: ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0. End to end, the three forces close a triangle.
forcetable.text: A force is an arrow: a size in newtons and a direction. Several forces on one body act as their sum, found by putting the arrows end to end, the parallelogram rule known to Stevin in 1586 and stated by Newton as the first corollary of his laws [1][2]. In practice one adds them by components, F cos θ along x and F sin θ along y. Here a ring is tied to three ropes that run over pulleys and carry 3, 4 and 5 kg, so each pulls with m g: 29.4, 39.2 and 49.1 N. From the centre, the ring slides along the sum of the three forces until both sums vanish. Forces in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 close a right triangle, so at equilibrium the two smaller ropes are at 90°. Seen from above; friction added so that the ring settles.
pulleys.title: Ropes and pulleys: Atwood's machine and the block and tackle
pulleys.mini: A rope pulls with the same tension all along. 3 kg against 2 kg over a pulley: a = g/5 = {{atA}} m/s², T = {{atT}} N. Four strands lift 40 kg with {{tkF}} N, for four times the rope.
pulleys.text: A rope only pulls, along itself, with the same tension all along when its mass and the pulleys' friction are negligible. In Atwood's machine (1784), two masses hang either side of a pulley [1]. On the heavy block m₁ a = m₁ g − T, on the light one m₂ a = T − m₂ g; adding the two removes T: a = (m₁ − m₂) g / (m₁ + m₂). With 3 and 2 kg, a = {{atA}} m/s² and T = {{atT}} N, between the two weights. In a block and tackle the load hangs on n strands of one rope, each with the same tension: four strands hold 40 kg ({{tkW}} N) with {{tkF}} N, and the rope must be pulled four metres for each metre the load rises. Force times distance is the same: pulleys trade force for distance and create no energy.
kick.title: Inertia: velocities add like forces
kick.mini: A puck sliding at 2 m/s gets a blow of {{kickJ}} N·s at 60°: v′ = v + J/m, {{kickV}} m/s at {{kickAng}}°. Two equal billiard balls, one at rest, always leave at 90° to each other.
kick.text: A moving body needs no force to keep moving: only a force changes its velocity [1]. A short blow is described by its impulse J, force times duration, which changes the velocity by J/m in the direction of the blow; the new velocity is the old one plus that arrow. A 170 g puck at 2 m/s struck with {{kickJ}} N·s at 60° to its path gains {{kickDv}} m/s that way and leaves at {{kickV}} m/s, {{kickAng}}° from its old path. In a collision the two bodies give each other equal and opposite impulses, so their total momentum is unchanged. For two equal balls, say a {{clM}} g ball A at {{clV}} m/s, slightly on a slant, hitting one at rest, split A's velocity along the line of centres at the impact (v_n = {{clVn}} m/s) and across it (v_t = {{clVt}} m/s). The contact force acts only along that line, equal and opposite on the two balls (third law); it removes v_n from A and gives it to the other ball, J = m v_n = {{clJ}} N·s (second law), and leaves v_t alone; billiard balls touch for about {{clTc}} ms, so the push peaks near {{clF}} N [2]. Momentum is unchanged; kinetic energy dips while the balls squeeze and comes back (an elastic collision); the balls part at 90°. Seen from above, without spin.
magnetic.title: Magnetic forces: always across the motion
magnetic.mini: A charge in a magnetic field feels F = q v × B, at right angles to its velocity: it circles. A proton at 1 km/s in 50 µT: r = {{lorP}} cm. A wire's field adds to the Earth's and turns a compass by {{compass}}°.
magnetic.text: In 1820 Ørsted saw a compass needle turn beside a wire carrying a current [1]. Lorentz wrote the force on a charge q moving at v in a field B as q v × B, perpendicular to both [2]. Never along the motion, it changes the direction and not the speed: in a uniform field the charge goes round a circle of radius m v / (|q| B). A proton at 1 km/s in 50 µT, the order of the Earth's field, circles on {{lorP}} cm, an electron on {{lorE}} mm [3]. Fields add as arrows: a straight wire with 5 A gives B = μ₀ I / (2π d) = {{wireB}} µT at 5 cm, and a compass just south of it turns towards the sum of that field and the Earth's horizontal 20 µT [4], by δ with tan δ = 20/20: {{compass}}°. Not to scale.
ballistic.title: Worked example: how far does a pushed steel ball go?
ballistic.mini: A {{bM}} kg steel ball pushed with 1,000 N at 30° for 0.1 s: force plus weight give {{bV0}} m/s at {{bA0}}°. It lands {{bRange}} m away in a vacuum, {{bRangeAir}} m in air.
ballistic.text: A steel ball 10 cm across weighs {{bM}} kg (7,850 kg/m³ [1]), so W = {{bW}} N. Pushed from the ground with 1,000 N at 30° for 0.1 s, it feels the push and its weight together: (866, 500 − {{bW}}) N, an acceleration of {{bAp}} m/s² at {{bApAng}}°, not 30°. After 0.1 s it moves at {{bV0}} m/s at {{bA0}}°. Then only its weight acts: horizontally the speed stays, vertically it falls by g each second, and the path is Galileo's parabola [2]; it lands {{bRange}} m away after {{bTf}} s, {{bHmax}} m high at the top. Air resistance adds a force ½ ρ C_D A v² against the motion, with ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and C_D ≈ 0.47 [3][4]: {{bDrag}} N at launch, {{bDragPct}} % of the weight, and the ball lands at {{bRangeAir}} m. Forgetting the weight during the push would give {{bNaiveR}} m. Spin, wind and a launch from the hand are left out.
frames.title: One collision seen from three inertial frames
frames.mini: A billiard ball hits another, seen from the floor, from a frame moving with its horizontal speed, and from one moving with the ball: velocities differ, the acceleration during the contact is the same. Momentum and energy are conserved in each.
frames.text: Velocities depend on the frame from which they are measured; changes of velocity do not. A billiard ball A moving at ({{clVx}}, {{clVy}}) m/s hits an identical ball at rest. Seen from a frame moving at u, every velocity is the floor's minus u: in a frame moving with A's horizontal speed, A only goes straight up before the impact; in a frame moving with A's whole velocity, A is at rest and the other ball comes at it. Subtracting the same u before and after leaves the change of velocity, and so the acceleration and the force, identical in all three: v′ = v − u gives Δv′ = Δv and F′ = F. Each frame finds momentum and kinetic energy conserved; the momentum differs from frame to frame. This is Galileo's relativity [1][2]. A frame that kept following A through the impact would not be inertial: A would never move in it, and a fictitious force would have to cancel the real push.
isum.title: The same impulse in one push, two, or a steady one
isum.mini: A ball at 2 m/s slowed by a steady wind, by two blows, or by one: same total ∫F dt = {{isJ}} N·s, same final velocity {{isVend}} m/s. Only the area under F(t) counts.
isum.text: Three 170 g balls roll at 2 m/s into a headwind. One is slowed by a steady force of {{isFw}} N for 2.5 s, one by two blows of 0.085 N·s, one by a single blow of {{isJ}} N·s. The force against time looks nothing alike, a long low strip or tall narrow spikes, but the area under it is the same, the impulse J = ∫F dt = Σ Jᵢ. The second law in this form, m Δv = ∫F dt [1], says the velocity changes by J/m whatever the shape: all three end at {{isVend}} m/s. Where they end up differs, because the velocity changed at different moments. The wind is taken as steady here; real air resistance grows with speed.
